senses.text: any of various large marine brown algae that are large seaweeds (order Laminariales) growing in cool waters — see also bladder kelp, bull kelp, giant kelp
examples: Only canopy-forming kelp are visible on the sea surface.
Kelps grow fast, drawing on all the minerals and vitamins and nutrients they can from the watershed and the sun.

senses.text: a mass or growth of large seaweeds
examples: The kelp near the outer islands teems with marine plants and animals in far greater abundance than it does closer to the coast …

senses.text: a blade (see blade:1) of kelp that is usually dried and used as food (as in sushi or soups)
a dietary supplement containing processed kelp
the ashes of seaweed used formerly especially as a source of iodine

phrases.meaning: a mottled sea bass (Paralabrax clathratus) that occurs along the Pacific coast of the U.S. and is an important sport fish
any of several large brown algae that have air bladders on the stipe or blade; especially : giant kelp

any of various very large brown algae (such as of the genera Durvillaea and Nereocystis); especially : a large kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana) found chiefly from Alaska to California that often forms dense stands, may reach a length of 130 feet (40 meters), and has a single large gas-filled air bladder at the end of the stipe from which arise two clusters of long narrow blades

a very large, fast-growing brown alga (Macrocystis pyrifera) of cool oceans that often grows in dense patches, may reach a length of 150 feet (45 meters), and has long stipes from which arise leaflike blades with gas-filled air bladders at their base —called also bladder kelp, giant bladder kelp

senses.text: a flammable hydrocarbon oil usually obtained by distillation of petroleum and used as a fuel, solvent, and thinner
to form by interlacing yarn or thread in a series of connected loops with needles
to link firmly or closely
to cause to grow together
examples: time and rest will knit a fractured bone

senses.text: to contract into wrinkles
to tie together
senses.label: chiefly dialectal

senses.text: to make knitted fabrics or objects
to become compact
to grow together
to become drawn together

entries.history: Middle English knitten, from Old English cnyttan; akin to Old English cnotta knot

phrases.meaning: a basic knitting stitch usually made with the yarn at the back of the work by inserting the right needle into the front part of a loop on the left needle from the left side, catching the yarn with the point of the right needle, and bringing it through the first loop to form a new loop
to move the eyebrows together in a way that shows that one is thinking about something or is worried, angry, etc.
having or made with a knitting stitch that produces a pattern resembling the twist of a usually two-ply cable
bound together by intimate social or cultural ties or by close economic or political ties

a knitted fabric (such as wool) made with a double set of needles to produce a double thickness of fabric with each thickness joined by interlocking stitches; also : an article of clothing made of such fabric
closely integrated and bound in love or friendship

senses.text: knit stitch
a knit fabric
knitwear
made from fabric formed by interlacing yarn or thread in a series of connected loops with needles made from a knitted fabric
involving connections or bonds between things or people
examples: a novel with a tightly knit plot
… a closely knit team of specialists and medical care professionals.

senses.text: an English-based creole spoken in Sierra Leone

entries.history: Krio, speaker of Krio, Krio language, perhaps from Yoruba Kiriyó Christian, ultimately from Portuguese crioulo Creole
